candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — hereditary cancer risk assessment, counseling referral, and preventive screening/risk management
candidate.educational_objective: Explain the preventive role of cancer genetic counseling for an unaffected person with a concerning family history, including informed testing decisions and individualized screening/risk-management planning without deterministic interpretation of results.

options.A: The counselor can review the client's personal and family history, estimate whether an inherited cancer syndrome may be present, discuss the benefits and limitations of genetic testing, and help the client make informed risk-management decisions.
options.B: Genetic counseling can determine with certainty whether the client will eventually develop cancer, even before any genetic testing is performed.
options.C: If genetic testing is negative, the client will no longer need cancer screening that would otherwise be recommended from personal and family risk factors.
options.D: Genetic counseling is useful only after a cancer diagnosis because people without cancer cannot be evaluated for inherited cancer susceptibility.

candidate.rationale: Cancer genetic counseling uses personal and family history to assess the likelihood of inherited cancer susceptibility and helps people understand the potential benefits, limitations, and implications of genetic testing before deciding whether to proceed. Counseling can also address enhanced screening and other risk-reduction options. Genetic information does not predict with certainty that cancer will or will not occur, and a negative result does not automatically eliminate screening or other management based on the person's remaining personal and family risk. People without cancer may appropriately be referred when their family history suggests hereditary cancer risk.
candidate.source_claim_supported: NCI and CDC state that genetic counseling reviews personal/family history, assesses the likelihood of inherited cancer risk, facilitates informed decisions about testing, and may address enhanced screening and risk-reduction strategies. A pathogenic variant increases risk but does not guarantee cancer, and a negative test may still leave management dependent on personal and family history.
